sections.title: Lesson 6.1: Nonqualified Accounts
sections.overview: Nonqualified accounts are accounts not part of a retirement plan; most are not tax-deferred. This lesson covers the principal account registrations: individual, joint (TIC and JTWROS), business, trust, custodial (UGMA/UTMA), and education savings accounts, along with key ownership features such as TOD designations and powers of attorney.
key_concepts: Individual account: one beneficial owner; sole control of investments and distributions; assets pass through estate at death absent other arrangements.
Joint account: two or more adult co-owners; all owners must sign new account form; checks payable to all and endorsed by all; mail to single address acceptable.
Tenants in Common (TIC): decedent's fractional interest passes to estate, not surviving tenants; specified percentages of ownership; account frozen at death until estate paperwork processed.
Joint Tenants with Right of Survivorship (JTWROS): undivided interest among all tenants; decedent's interest passes to surviving tenant(s); common for married couples.

Transfer on Death (TOD): allows account assets to pass directly to named beneficiary at death; avoids probate but not estate tax; available on individual and JTWROS accounts (effective after last survivor dies for joint).
Power of Attorney (POA): written authorization required for any non-owner to exercise authority; POA granted to a person, not a firm; fiduciary duty to owner; cancelled at death of either party.
Full POA (FPOA): permits deposits, withdrawals, and investment decisions; RR holding FPOA on non-family account is unusual and typically not approved.
Limited POA (LPOA): permits trading (buy/sell) but no withdrawal of assets; also called limited trading authorization.
Durable POA: survives incapacity of grantor but still ends at death of either party.

Business accounts: sole proprietor (may use d/b/a name), partnership (requires written partnership agreement; amended yearly if changes), corporate (requires corporate charter and corporate resolution).
Corporate resolution: identifies legal right to open the account, any investment limitations, and designated officers authorized to enter orders.
Margin in business accounts: partnership agreement or corporate charter must not prohibit it.
Trust roles: grantor/settlor (places assets in trust), trustee (manages), beneficiary (benefits). Three aspects of ownership can be split.
Living trust: created and funded during grantor's lifetime (most common test focus). Decedent's trust: funded after grantor's death via will/estate.
Revocable trust: can be modified/revoked by grantor; assets remain in grantor's estate; grantor often serves as trustee and beneficiary.
Irrevocable trust: cannot be modified; assets may be removed from grantor's estate; grantor cannot serve as trustee or beneficiary if removal from estate is desired.
Trust must specifically allow margin to open a margin account.
Custodial accounts (UGMA/UTMA): one custodian, one minor; custodian has full control; minor is beneficial owner (minor's SSN used; taxed at minor's rate).

Custodial account restrictions: cash account only; no margin; no pledging as collateral; reinvest cash within reasonable time; no commodities futures, naked options, or high-risk securities; covered call writing allowed; rights/warrants must be exercised or sold.
UTMA vs UGMA: UTMA allows real estate; UTMA may extend custodianship to age 25 (21 in some states); UGMA ends at age of majority; nearly all states now use UTMA.

Coverdell ESA (Education IRA): after-tax contributions up to $2,000/year per beneficiary until age 18; tax-deferred growth; tax-free distributions for qualified K-12 or college expenses; nonqualified distributions taxed plus 10% penalty on earnings; must be distributed by age 30 or rolled to another beneficiary.
Fiduciary types: trustee, executor, administrator, guardian, custodian, receiver, conservator.

Fiduciary account rules: proper authorization/court documents; no speculative transactions; margin only if legal documents permit; prudent investor rule applies; fiduciary may not share in profits but may charge reasonable fee.
Numbered accounts: permitted for privacy in exceptional circumstances; firm must keep record of true owners.
rules: All POAs (including durable) terminate at death of either the grantor (account owner) or the appointed attorney.
Joint account checks must be payable to and endorsed by all tenants.
TIC: percentages of ownership specified; if not specified, assumed equal.
JTWROS: all owners have undivided interest in entire account.
Corporate account requires: corporate charter (proof of existence) + corporate resolution (authorizes opening and designates traders).
Custodial account: one custodian, one minor; only individuals (not entities) may be custodian; donor may name themselves or another as custodian.
Custodial accounts must be cash accounts (no margin, no pledging).
Coverdell ESA contribution limit: $2,000 per year per beneficiary; phased out at higher income levels.
Coverdell ESA age limits: contributions until age 18; funds must be used by age 30 (or rolled to another beneficiary).
Custodial account taxation: under minor's SSN at minor's tax rate; custodian responsible for ensuring taxes are paid.
If minor beneficiary dies, custodial account passes to minor's estate (not custodian's).
Irrevocable trust: grantor cannot be trustee or beneficiary if assets are to be excluded from grantor's estate.
mnemonics: TIC = Tenants In Common = each person specifies a piece (percentage); Inheritance goes to Estate.
JTWROS = 'Surviving spouse wins' — decedent's share goes to survivors.
POA dies when either Party Or Attorney dies.
Custodial accounts: One Custodian, One Minor, One SSN (the minor's).
Three roles of a trust: 'GTB' — Grantor, Trustee, Beneficiary.

sections.title: Lesson 6.2: Qualified Accounts
sections.overview: Qualified accounts are tax-advantaged retirement vehicles. IRAs (traditional and Roth) are self-funded retirement accounts with annual contribution limits; employer-sponsored plans divide broadly into defined benefit (pension) plans and defined contribution plans. This lesson details contribution, rollover, transfer, and distribution rules along with RMD requirements.
key_concepts: Traditional IRA contributions: must come from earned income (salary, wages, tips); no age limit; deadline is tax filing deadline (typically April 15) of following year.
Catch-up contribution: $1,000 additional for individuals age 50 and older.
Traditional IRA contributions may be tax-deductible; deduction phases out at higher AGI if individual is covered by employer retirement plan.
Earnings in IRAs grow tax-deferred regardless of contribution deductibility.
Permitted IRA investments: stocks, bonds, mutual funds, UITs, government securities, U.S.-minted gold/silver coins, annuities.
Prohibited IRA investments: collectibles (antiques, gems, rare coins, art, stamps), life insurance.
Prohibited IRA practices: short sales, speculative options, margin trading; municipal securities are inappropriate (tax-free in a tax-deferred account). Covered call writing is permitted.
Rollover: customer takes possession of assets and redeposits to another qualified account within 60 calendar days; one rollover per rolling 12-month period per person.
Transfer (custodian-to-custodian): unlimited; moving from employer plan to IRA (direct rollover) is technically a transfer.
Traditional IRA distributions: penalty-free after age 59½; taxed as ordinary income. Distributions before 59½ incur 10% penalty plus ordinary income tax.
10% penalty exceptions: death, disability, first-time home purchase (up to $10,000), education expenses, medical premiums for unemployed, excess medical expenses.

RMDs begin in the year the account owner turns 72; due by December 31 each year (first may be delayed to April 1 of following year, but then a second RMD is also required by December 31 that same year).
Failure to take RMD: 50% penalty on shortfall.
Aggregate RMD for multiple IRAs: total computed across accounts; may be withdrawn from any one or combination.
Roth IRA contributions: same limits as traditional (combined limit across both); not tax-deductible; income limits phase out eligibility; no age limit; must be from earned income.
Roth IRA distributions: principal always tax-free; qualified distributions of earnings are tax-free.
Qualified Roth distribution requires: account held 5 years AND owner is 59½ (or death, disability, first-time home purchase up to $10,000).
Roth IRA: no RMDs during owner's lifetime.
Roth IRA suitability: ideal for younger investors (longer tax-free growth) and lower-income taxpayers (current deduction has little value).
Excess IRA contributions: 6% penalty per year until corrected.
Defined Benefit Plan (pension): defines retiree benefit by formula (years of service × percentage × salary); employer bears investment risk; actuary determines required contributions.
Private pensions pay fixed benefits (purchasing power risk to retiree); government pensions often include COLA.
Defined Contribution Plans: define contribution amount, not benefit; employee bears investment risk; balance is portable.
Defined contribution plan types: 401(k), 403(b), profit-sharing, money purchase, SIMPLE.
rules: IRA contributions must be from earned income.
Annual contribution limit applies in aggregate across traditional and Roth IRAs combined.
Rollover time limit: 60 calendar days; limit of one rollover per rolling 12-month period per individual.
Premature distribution penalty: 10% additional tax on amounts withdrawn before age 59½ (with listed exceptions).
RMD start age: 72; deadline December 31 (first RMD may be delayed to April 1 of following year).
RMD shortfall penalty: 50%.
Excess contribution penalty: 6% per year until withdrawn.
Roth qualified distribution: 5-year holding period AND age 59½ (or death/disability/first-time home).
Life insurance and collectibles prohibited in IRAs.
formulas: Defined Benefit example: Annual benefit = years of service × benefit percentage × average final salary (subject to plan cap)
Excess contribution penalty = 6% × excess amount × number of years uncorrected
Premature distribution tax = ordinary income tax + 10% penalty
mnemonics: Rollover rule: '60 days, 1 per year' (60 calendar days, one rollover per rolling 12-month period).
IRA Don'ts: 'CLIMB' — Collectibles, Life insurance, Insurance contracts, Margin, Bad (speculative) options.

sections.title: Lesson 6.3: Account Features
sections.overview: This lesson covers the principal account features — cash, margin, fee-based, discretionary, and wrap accounts — along with the documents, regulatory requirements, and trading authorizations associated with each. Key distinctions include solicited vs. unsolicited trades and the three elements that define discretion.
key_concepts: Cash account: full payment required by settlement; payment expected by end of day on settlement date; Regulation T allows up to two business days after standard settlement.
Accounts that MUST be cash accounts: IRAs and other retirement plans, UGMA/UTMA custodial accounts.
Margin account: customer borrows from BD to purchase securities (long margin) or borrows stock to sell short (short margin).
Margin advantages: increased buying power, leveraged returns (and leveraged losses).
Hypothecation: customer pledges securities as collateral for margin loan (signed via margin agreement).
Rehypothecation: BD repledges customer securities to a bank to obtain financing (governed by Regulation U).
Commingling: customer securities may not be commingled with firm's securities; may be commingled with other customers' securities only with written consent.

Margin permissions: most individual and joint accounts allow margin; corporate/partnership require document not prohibit margin; trusts must specifically authorize margin; IRAs and UGMA/UTMA may never have margin.

Three margin forms: Credit Agreement (mandatory) — terms of credit/interest; Hypothecation Agreement (mandatory) — pledges securities as collateral; Loan Consent Agreement (optional) — permits firm to lend customer securities to others.

Margin risk disclosure document: must be provided when account opened and annually thereafter; discloses risks including no choice in which securities are sold on maintenance call, possible loss exceeding deposit, no entitlement to extensions, and firm may raise house requirements without notice.
Securities eligible for margin purchase: exchange-listed stocks/bonds, Nasdaq stocks, FRB-approved OTC issues, warrants.
Not eligible for margin purchase or collateral: options, rights, non-NMS OTC issues not approved by FRB, insurance contracts.
Mutual funds and new issues: not marginable initially but become acceptable collateral after 30 days.
Exempt securities (from Regulation T but still required for initial deposit calc): U.S. Treasuries, agency issues, municipal securities.
Initial margin deposit: greater of Regulation T (50%) or FINRA minimum ($2,000 or 100% of purchase if less than $2,000).
Maintenance call: FINRA minimum equity is 25% for long accounts, 30% for short accounts; house requirements may be higher.
Cash vs. margin terminology: 'margin' = required equity deposit; 'marginable' = securities usable as collateral.
Fee-based account: flat or percentage-of-AUM fee replacing per-trade commissions; suitable for active traders, not buy-and-hold investors.
Solicited trade: representative or firm recommended the security; ticket marked 'solicited'.
Unsolicited trade: customer's own idea without firm input; ticket marked 'unsolicited'.
Discretionary trade: RR chooses one or more of the three As (Action, Amount, Asset) without specific customer instruction.
Time and price discretion only is NOT considered true discretion.
Discretionary account requirements: written customer authorization, written principal approval, and prompt principal review of each discretionary trade.
Discretion is granted to the RR personally — terminates if RR leaves the firm or dies.

Wrap account: bundled services (advice, management, execution, administration) for single fee (usually % of AUM); generally an investment advisory account subject to Investment Advisers Act of 1940; firm must register as investment adviser and disclose that services could be obtained separately for less.
rules: Regulation T: 50% initial margin requirement; payment due no later than two business days after standard settlement.
FINRA initial minimum: $2,000 (or 100% of purchase if less); customer deposits greater of Reg T or FINRA minimum.
FINRA maintenance: 25% long, 30% short (minimums; houses may set higher).
Regulation U: governs bank loans to BDs secured by customer collateral (rehypothecation).
Margin opening documents required: credit agreement and hypothecation agreement (mandatory); loan consent (optional).
Margin risk disclosure required at account opening and annually.
Discretionary trades require: prior written customer authorization, written principal approval of the authorization, and prompt principal review.
Revocation of discretion: customer must revoke in writing.
Time/price-only authority is not discretion under FINRA Rule 3260.
Solicited/unsolicited marking on order tickets is mandatory; mismarking is a violation.
formulas: Initial margin deposit = greater of (50% × purchase price) OR (lesser of $2,000 and 100% of purchase price)
Long maintenance equity requirement = 25% × Long Market Value (FINRA minimum)
Short maintenance equity requirement = 30% × Short Market Value (FINRA minimum)
Return on margin purchase = (Gain or Loss) / Initial Equity Deposited (vs. cash return = Gain or Loss / Total Purchase Price)
mnemonics: Three As of Discretion: Action, Amount, Asset (if RR picks any one without instruction = discretion).
Margin forms: 'CHL' — Credit, Hypothecation (both required), Loan consent (optional).
Initial deposit rule: 'Greater of 50% or $2,000' (but never more than 100% of purchase).
Cannot-margin accounts: 'RICK' — Retirement, IRAs, Custodial (UGMA/UTMA), Know your document (trusts must specify).
